title: The Axioms of Probability

intro.x: The classical rule $\abs{A}/\abs{\Omega}$ works only for finite, symmetric situations. In 1933 Kolmogorov showed that all of probability can be built on a short list of axioms. This chapter states them, derives their consequences, and proves the two most useful computational tools: inclusion–exclusion and continuity of probability.

blocks.x: When $\Omega$ is finite or countable, every subset can be an event. In general we need to choose a collection $\F$ of subsets of $\Omega$ that are allowed to be events, and this collection must be closed under the operations we use to combine events.
A collection $\F$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is a $\sigma$-algebra (or $\sigma$-field) if
$\Omega\in\F$;
if $A\in\F$ then $A^c\in\F$;
if $A_1,A_2,\dots\in\F$ then $\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i\in\F$.

By De Morgan’s laws (Theorem 1.4), $\F$ is then also closed under countable intersections, and $\emptyset=\Omega^c\in\F$. Taking $A_{n+1}=A_{n+2}=\dots=\emptyset$ shows that $\F$ is closed under finite unions as well.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: why not simply use all subsets?

blocks.x: For finite or countable $\Omega$ we can, and we will, take $\F=2^\Omega$, the collection of all subsets. For $\Omega=[0,1]$ one cannot assign a length consistently to every subset: there exist sets (Vitali sets) for which no assignment of “length” is compatible with countable additivity and translation invariance. The $\sigma$-algebra restricts attention to the sets that can be measured. This is a technicality that rarely matters in computation; we return to it in Chapter 15. For now, read “event” as “measurable subset” and note that every set built from intervals by countable unions, intersections and complements is an event.
Let $\Omega$ be a set and $\F$ a $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$. A probability measure is a function $\Prob:\F\to\R$ such that
(Non-negativity) $\Prob(A)\ge 0$ for every $A\in\F$;
(Normalisation) $\Prob(\Omega)=1$;
(Countable additivity) if $A_1,A_2,\dots\in\F$ are pairwise disjoint, then
\Prob\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i\Bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^\infty\Prob(A_i).
The triple $(\Omega,\F,\Prob)$ is called a probability space.
These axioms say nothing about how to choose $\Prob$ in a given problem; that is a modelling decision. They only say what any sensible assignment must satisfy.

Let $\Omega=\{\omega_1,\omega_2,\dots\}$ be finite or countable and let $p_1,p_2,\dots\ge 0$ satisfy $\sum_ip_i=1$. Defining $\Prob(A)=\sum_{i:\omega_i\in A}p_i$ gives a probability measure on $\F=2^\Omega$: non-negativity and normalisation are immediate, and countable additivity follows because a sum of non-negative terms may be rearranged and grouped freely. The classical definition is the case $p_i=1/\abs\Omega$.
Let $(\Omega,\F,\Prob)$ be a probability space and $A,B\in\F$. Then
$\Prob(\emptyset)=0$;
(finite additivity) if $A\cap B=\emptyset$ then $\Prob(A\cup B)=\Prob(A)+\Prob(B)$; more generally this holds for any finite number of pairwise disjoint events;
$\Prob(A^c)=1-\Prob(A)$;
(monotonicity) if $A\subseteq B$ then $\Prob(A)\le\Prob(B)$, and $\Prob(B\setminus A)=\Prob(B)-\Prob(A)$;
$0\le\Prob(A)\le 1$;
$\Prob(A\cup B)=\Prob(A)+\Prob(B)-\Prob(A\cap B)$.

(i) Apply A3 to the sequence $\emptyset,\emptyset,\dots$ (pairwise disjoint, with union $\emptyset$): $\Prob(\emptyset)=\sum_{i=1}^\infty\Prob(\emptyset)$. A real number $x$ with $x=\sum_{i\ge 1}x$ must be $0$, because $x>0$ would give $+\infty$ and $x\ge0$ by A1.
(ii) Apply A3 to $A,B,\emptyset,\emptyset,\dots$ and use (i). The case of $m$ events is identical.
(iii) $A$ and $A^c$ are disjoint with union $\Omega$, so by (ii) and A2, $1=\Prob(A)+\Prob(A^c)$.
(iv) If $A\subseteq B$, then $B=A\cup(B\setminus A)$ is a disjoint union, so $\Prob(B)=\Prob(A)+\Prob(B\setminus A)\ge\Prob(A)$ by A1.
(v) The upper bound is (iv) with $B=\Omega$; the lower bound is A1.

(vi) Write $A\cup B=A\cup(B\setminus A)$, a disjoint union, and $B=(A\cap B)\cup(B\setminus A)$, also disjoint. Then $\Prob(A\cup B)=\Prob(A)+\Prob(B\setminus A)$ and $\Prob(B)=\Prob(A\cap B)+\Prob(B\setminus A)$. Subtract the second equation from the first.
For any events $A_1,A_2,\dots$ (finitely or countably many, not necessarily disjoint),
\Prob\Bigl(\bigcup_iA_i\Bigr)\le\sum_i\Prob(A_i).

Define $B_1=A_1$ and $B_i=A_i\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{i-1})$ for $i\ge 2$. The $B_i$ are pairwise disjoint, $B_i\subseteq A_i$, and $\bigcup_iB_i=\bigcup_iA_i$. (If $\omega\in\bigcup_iA_i$, let $i$ be the smallest index with $\omega\in A_i$; then $\omega\in B_i$.) By countable additivity and monotonicity,
\Prob\Bigl(\bigcup_iA_i\Bigr)=\sum_i\Prob(B_i)\le\sum_i\Prob(A_i).
The union bound requires no independence assumption, which makes it one of the most widely applicable inequalities in probability.
Part (vi) of Proposition 2.4 computes $\Prob(A\cup B)$ for two events. For $n$ events the formula alternates between adding and subtracting intersections.
For events $A_1,\dots,A_n$ in a discrete probability space,

\Prob\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^nA_i\Bigr)=\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^{k+1}S_k,
\qquad
S_k=\sum_{1\le i_1<\dots<i_k\le n}\Prob\bigl(A_{i_1}\cap\dots\cap A_{i_k}\bigr).

We give the proof for the discrete setting of Example 2.3, where $\Prob(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}p(\omega)$ (the result holds on any probability space, and a proof by induction on $n$ using Proposition 2.4(vi) is possible as well). It suffices to show that every outcome $\omega$ contributes the same weight $p(\omega)$ to both sides, or contributes nothing to both.

If $\omega$ lies in none of the $A_i$, it contributes nothing to either side. Otherwise suppose $\omega$ lies in exactly $m\ge1$ of the events. On the left it contributes $p(\omega)$. On the right, $\omega$ belongs to the intersection $A_{i_1}\cap\dots\cap A_{i_k}$ exactly when all of $i_1,\dots,i_k$ are among the $m$ events containing $\omega$; there are $\binom mk$ such index sets. So the total contribution of $\omega$ to the right side is

p(\omega)\sum_{k=1}^m(-1)^{k+1}\binom mk
=p(\omega)\Bigl[1-\sum_{k=0}^m(-1)^k\binom mk\Bigr]=p(\omega)(1-0)=p(\omega),
by Corollary 1.15. The two sides agree.
With $S_k$ as above, the partial sums alternately overestimate and underestimate:

\sum_{k=1}^{j}(-1)^{k+1}S_k\ \ge\ \Prob\Bigl(\bigcup_iA_i\Bigr)\ \text{ for odd } j,
\qquad
\sum_{k=1}^{j}(-1)^{k+1}S_k\ \le\ \Prob\Bigl(\bigcup_iA_i\Bigr)\ \text{ for even } j.
We use the same outcome-by-outcome argument. First an identity: for integers $m\ge1$ and $0\le j\le m-1$,
\sum_{k=0}^{j}(-1)^k\binom mk=(-1)^j\binom{m-1}{j}.

Proof by Pascal’s rule (Theorem 1.13), writing $\binom mk=\binom{m-1}k+\binom{m-1}{k-1}$ for $k\ge 1$: the sum becomes $\sum_{k=0}^j(-1)^k\binom{m-1}k+\sum_{k=1}^j(-1)^k\binom{m-1}{k-1}$, and the second sum equals $-\sum_{k=0}^{j-1}(-1)^k\binom{m-1}{k}$. The two sums cancel except for the term $k=j$ of the first, which is $(-1)^j\binom{m-1}j$.
Now consider an outcome lying in exactly $m\ge 1$ of the events. Its contribution to the partial sum up to $j$ is, by (2.1) (and trivially if $j\ge m$, where the full alternating sum applies),
p(\omega)\sum_{k=1}^{j}(-1)^{k+1}\binom mk=p(\omega)\Bigl[1-(-1)^j\binom{m-1}{j}\Bigr].
For $j$ odd the bracket equals $1+\binom{m-1}{j}\ge 1$, and for $j$ even it equals $1-\binom{m-1}{j}\le1$. Summing over $\omega$ gives the claims.

$n$ letters are put at random into $n$ addressed envelopes, one per envelope. What is the probability that no letter lands in its own envelope? Let $\Omega$ be the set of $n!$ permutations, all equally likely, and let $A_i$ be the event that letter $i$ is correctly placed (position $i$ is fixed). For any $k$ distinct indices, the number of permutations fixing all of them is $(n-k)!$, so

\Prob(A_{i_1}\cap\dots\cap A_{i_k})=\frac{(n-k)!}{n!},
\qquad
S_k=\binom nk\frac{(n-k)!}{n!}=\frac1{k!}.
By inclusion–exclusion,

\Prob(\text{no match})=1-\Prob\Bigl(\bigcup_iA_i\Bigr)
=1-\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k!}=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.

This is the partial sum of the series $e^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge 0}(-1)^k/k!$. By the alternating series estimate the error is at most $1/(n+1)!$, so already for $n=7$ the answer agrees with $e^{-1}\approx0.3679$ to four decimal places. Remarkably, the limit does not depend on $n$.

When asked for the probability that none of several events occurs, and the events are symmetric (each $k$-fold intersection has probability depending only on $k$), inclusion–exclusion gives a closed form quickly, as in the matching problem. The same structure appears in the coupon-collector and “everyone has a different birthday” problems.
Countable additivity is the axiom that connects probability to limits. Its most useful form is continuity.

A sequence of events $A_1,A_2,\dots$ is increasing if $A_1\subseteq A_2\subseteq\cdots$, with limit $A=\bigcup_nA_n$ (written $A_n\uparrow A$). It is decreasing if $A_1\supseteq A_2\supseteq\cdots$, with limit $A=\bigcap_nA_n$ (written $A_n\downarrow A$).
If $A_n\uparrow A$ or $A_n\downarrow A$, then $\Prob(A_n)\to\Prob(A)$.
Increasing case. Set $B_1=A_1$ and $B_n=A_n\setminus A_{n-1}$ for $n\ge 2$. The $B_n$ are pairwise disjoint, $A_n=B_1\cup\dots\cup B_n$, and $A=\bigcup_nB_n$. By countable additivity,

\Prob(A)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\Prob(B_n)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=1}^N\Prob(B_n)
=\lim_{N\to\infty}\Prob(A_N),
where the last step is finite additivity.
Decreasing case. If $A_n\downarrow A$ then $A_n^c\uparrow A^c$ (by De Morgan’s laws). By the increasing case, $\Prob(A_n^c)\to\Prob(A^c)$, that is, $1-\Prob(A_n)\to1-\Prob(A)$.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: the decreasing case needs a finite total mass

blocks.x: The decreasing case used $\Prob(\Omega)=1<\infty$. For measures with infinite total mass (for example length on $\R$) continuity from above can fail: $A_n=[n,\infty)$ decreases to $\emptyset$ but each has infinite length. Probability measures escape this problem precisely because of normalisation.

Toss a fair coin repeatedly. Let $A_n$ be the event that the first $n$ tosses are all heads. Then $\Prob(A_n)=2^{-n}$ and $A_n\downarrow A$, where $A$ is the event that every toss is heads. By continuity, $\Prob(A)=\lim_n2^{-n}=0$. The sequence $HHH\cdots$ is a perfectly possible outcome, yet it has probability zero.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: probability zero does not mean impossible

blocks.x: Example 2.11 shows that an event can be possible and still have probability $0$. Likewise, probability $1$ does not mean certain. We say an event holds almost surely (a.s.) if it has probability $1$. This distinction becomes unavoidable for continuous random variables, where every single value has probability zero but some value must occur.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: why countable, and not merely finite, additivity

blocks.x: Finite additivity gives no control over limits of events; countable additivity is exactly what makes Theorem 2.10 true. It also rules out some tempting models. There is no way to choose a natural number “uniformly at random”: if $\Prob(\{n\})=c$ for all $n\in\N$, then countable additivity gives $1=\Prob(\N)=\sum_{n}c$, which equals $0$ if $c=0$ and $\infty$ if $c>0$, a contradiction either way. (If only finite additivity is demanded, uniform “distributions” on $\N$ do exist, but they fail to behave well under limits, which is why the standard theory does not allow them.)

blocks.name: Corollary
blocks.title: Countable unions as limits of finite unions

blocks.x: For any events $A_1,A_2,\dots$ we have $\Prob(\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\Prob(\bigcup_{i=1}^NA_i)$.
The sets $C_N=\bigcup_{i=1}^NA_i$ increase to $\bigcup_iA_i$; apply Theorem 2.10.
Show that if $\Prob(A)=0.6$ and $\Prob(B)=0.7$, then $0.3\le\Prob(A\cap B)\le0.6$, and show that both bounds can be attained.
Prove the Bonferroni-type bound $\Prob(\bigcap_iA_i)\ge1-\sum_i\Prob(A_i^c)$.
Prove inclusion–exclusion for three events by repeated use of Proposition 2.4(vi), and then prove the general theorem by induction on $n$.
(Derangements) Let $D_n$ be the number of permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with no fixed point. Show $D_n=n!\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k/k!$ and verify that $D_n$ is the nearest integer to $n!/e$ for $n\ge 1$.
Show that the probability that exactly one of the events $A_1,\dots,A_n$ occurs equals $S_1-2S_2+3S_3-\cdots+(-1)^{n+1}nS_n$.
Let $\F$ be a $\sigma$-algebra. Prove that $\F$ is closed under countable intersections and under set difference.

A fair coin is tossed repeatedly. Use continuity of probability to show that the probability that heads never appears is $0$, and that the probability that the first head appears at some finite toss is $1$.

Show that a function satisfying A1, A2 and finite additivity (but not countable additivity) is a probability measure if and only if it is continuous at $\emptyset$, meaning $\Prob(A_n)\to0$ whenever $A_n\downarrow\emptyset$.

(Challenge) Show that there is no probability measure on $(\N,2^\N)$ with $\Prob(\{n\})=c$ for all $n$, but that for $p_n=2^{-n}$ the construction of Example 2.3 gives a legitimate geometric model for the first head in repeated tosses (Example 1.2(d)).
